analogy.p: Imagine living in a house where the tap only runs for a few minutes once or twice a year and the heating is at full blast all day but off at night. You would collect and store water in tanks (cactus stems), keep the curtains drawn and stay in cool rooms during the day (nocturnal animals in burrows), and wear light clothes that reflect sunlight (pale fur). You would also use as little as possible by closing lids and avoiding waste (waxy skin and spines). The analogy breaks down because a house owner can choose to move, whereas desert organisms must be adapted by evolution over many generations, and their body features also have to work automatically.
analogy.t: Living in a house with a very low water budget

bullets: **Hot desert** = an environment with **very low rainfall** (usually less than 250 mm a year) and **high temperatures**.
Know the **global distribution** around 15 to 35 degrees north and south of the Equator.
Know the **climate**: low, unreliable rainfall; very hot days; large daily temperature range.
Know the **soils** and **vegetation**, including how plants are adapted (**xerophytes**).
Know **animal adaptations**, for example camel, fennec fox, kangaroo rat.
Be able to **link physical features to adaptations**: explain WHY each adaptation helps survival.
Use a named case study for **opportunities and challenges** of development.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8035 asks you to know the **characteristics of hot desert environments**: where they are, their **climate, soils, vegetation and animals**, and how plants and animals have **adapted** to the extreme conditions. You also need to understand the **opportunities and challenges** of development in a hot desert, shown with a case study of one hot desert (for example the Thar Desert in India or the Sahara). In the exam, 'describe' questions test the facts and patterns, while 'explain' questions test how adaptations help organisms **survive**.

bullets: At the Equator the Sun is overhead, so air is heated, rises and cools, forming clouds and heavy rain (the rainforest belt).
The dry high-level air spreads north and south and **descends** at about 30 degrees latitude.
Descending air **warms and dries**, so clouds do not form: a belt of **high pressure** (subtropical high).
Clear skies mean **strong sunshine** by day and **rapid heat loss** at night.
Other factors: **continentality** (far from the sea, little moisture), **rain-shadow** effects (mountains block rain), and **cold ocean currents** (such as the Atacama and Namib coasts).
Not all deserts are in the 15 to 35 degree belt, but the **sinking air** explanation is the main one for the exam.
You can **describe** the pattern: 'a band either side of the Tropics, mostly on western sides and in continental interiors'.

Figure 1 shows the **Hadley cell** in cross-section: heating at the Equator, rising air, high-level flow, sinking at about 30 degrees and surface winds returning, so the hot deserts lie on the ground below the sinking air (about 15 to 35 degrees north and south).
core.h: Where hot deserts are found and why
core.p: Hot deserts are found mainly in a belt around **15 to 35 degrees north and south** of the Equator, close to the **Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn**. Examples are the **Sahara** in North Africa, the **Arabian Desert**, the **Thar** (India and Pakistan), the **Kalahari and Namib** in southern Africa, the **Atacama** in South America and the **Australian deserts**. They occur here because of the **global atmospheric circulation**: air rises at the Equator, cools and loses its moisture as rain, then moves away and **sinks** at about 30 degrees north and south. Sinking air warms up, so water cannot condense into cloud, giving **high pressure**, clear skies and very little rain.

bullets: **Annual rainfall below 250 mm** (compare the UK at around 800 to 1,200 mm in many places).
Rainfall is **unreliable** and **irregular**: some years nearly none.
Rain tends to fall in **heavy, short storms**, causing **flash floods** and **runoff** with little infiltration.
**Evaporation** greatly exceeds rainfall, so water is rapidly lost from the surface.
Clear skies and **low humidity** mean little cloud cover.
This is why plants must **store water** or **get it deep underground**.
In a graph, rainfall bars are **very small** and may be zero for several months.
Figure 2 (illustrative data) shows how to read a climate graph: rainfall as bars on the right axis, temperature as a line on the left axis; the total rainfall here is 31 mm, far below 250 mm.
core.p: The defining feature of a hot desert is **aridity**: there is very little **precipitation**, normally under **250 mm per year**, and it is often **unreliable**. Rain may fall in short, intense storms, then nothing for months or even years. Because the ground is bare and hard, this rain can cause **flash floods** that run off quickly instead of soaking in. Evaporation is much higher than rainfall, so the land stays dry, and this lack of water is the main limiting factor for living things.

bullets: Daytime maximum often **over 40 degrees Celsius** in summer (higher than 50 degrees at times in the hottest deserts).
Night-time minimum may fall to **near 0 degrees Celsius**.
**Diurnal range** is large: **20 to 30 degrees** or more.
Reasons: clear skies, **little cloud** and **low humidity** so heat is lost quickly after sunset.
**Dry, bare surfaces** heat up and cool down faster than moist or vegetated surfaces.
Descriptions should use **figures** from the graph: name the **highest** and **lowest** values and the **range**.
Temperature affects **water loss** from plants and animals, so adaptations focus on keeping cool and saving water.

Annual temperature range = highest monthly mean minus lowest monthly mean; in Figure 2 this is 36 - 14 = 22 degrees Celsius. The **diurnal** (day-night) range is usually even larger than this in a hot desert.
core.p: Hot deserts have **very high daytime temperatures**, often **above 40 degrees Celsius** in the hottest months, because the clear skies allow intense **insolation** (incoming solar radiation). At night the same clear, dry air lets heat escape quickly (**radiation to space**), so temperatures can fall to near **0 degrees** or lower. This produces a very large **diurnal (daily) temperature range** of 20 degrees or more. Seasonal change is smaller in tropical deserts, with hot summers and warm winters, while some deserts at higher latitudes have cold winters.

bullets: Soils are **coarse, thin and dry**, with **little humus** (organic matter).
**Low fertility** because there is little leaf litter or decomposition.
**Rapid drainage** in sandy soils; **runoff** on hard, baked surfaces.
**Salt crusts** can form where water evaporates leaving salts behind.
Wind causes **erosion and deposition**, forming dunes.
Only about a **fifth** of the Sahara is sand dune; much is rock and gravel.
Soil conditions limit the **vegetation** and **farming** unless water is supplied.
core.p: Desert soils are generally **thin, coarse, sandy or stony** and **low in organic matter** because there are few plants and little decay. Without vegetation, **nutrients** are low. Water drains rapidly through coarse soils, and where evaporation is high, **salts** can be drawn up and form crusts on the surface (**salinisation**). The ground is often hard, so when rain does fall it runs off rather than soaking in. Desert landscapes include **sand dunes (ergs)**, **stony plains (regs)** and **rocky highlands**, so not all deserts are sandy.

bullets: **Cactus**: thick, fleshy stem **stores water**; **spines** instead of leaves reduce the surface area for water loss and protect against animals; **waxy cuticle** reduces evaporation.
**Shallow, extensive roots** (cactus) take in water quickly after rare rain.
**Long tap roots** (for example mesquite) reach deep water tables (tens of metres in some cases).
**Small or reduced leaves** and thick waxy coating reduce **transpiration**.
Some plants open their pores (**stomata**) only at night to cut water loss.
**Seeds** can lie **dormant** for years and germinate and flower quickly after rain (ephemerals).
**Light-coloured or hairy** surfaces reflect sunlight and trap moist air.
Vegetation is **sparse and scattered**, so ground cover is low.
Figure 3 locates each adaptation on a cactus and a mesquite tree: spines, waxy cuticle, ribbed water-storing stem, shallow wide roots, small leaflets and a tap root reaching the water table.
core.p: Plants in hot deserts are called **xerophytes** because they are adapted to dry conditions. Because water is scarce and evaporation is high, their adaptations aim to **collect, store and conserve water**. Some have **deep tap roots** that reach groundwater far below, others have **shallow, wide-spreading roots** that quickly absorb rain from a large area after a storm. Many have **small, thick, waxy leaves or spines** to reduce **transpiration**, and some **store water** in swollen stems. Vegetation is **sparse** and widely spaced so plants do not compete for scarce water.

bullets: **Camel**: **hump stores fat** (an energy store, not water); **wide, flat feet** stop sinking in sand; **long eyelashes** and **closable nostrils** keep out sand; can **tolerate large water loss** and drink a large amount quickly; thick coat insulates against heat.
**Fennec fox**: **large ears** radiate heat and lose body heat; **pale fur** reflects sunlight; **nocturnal** and lives in **burrows**; furry feet protect from hot sand.
**Kangaroo rat**: gets water from **seeds** (metabolic water); produces **very concentrated urine**; **nocturnal** and burrows; may never drink.
**Reptiles** (lizards and snakes): **scaly, waterproof skin** reduces water loss; **shelter** under rocks; **sidewinding** reduces contact with hot sand.
**Desert tortoise**: stores water in its bladder and shelters in burrows.
**Behavioural**: nocturnal activity, resting in shade, migrating to find water.
Always **link** the feature to the problem: 'large ears so heat is lost, which helps keep the body cool'.

Figure 4 shows structural adaptations (camel: hump of fat, wide flat feet, long eyelashes; fennec fox: large ears, pale fur, furry feet) and the behavioural adaptation of being nocturnal and sheltering in burrows by day.
core.h: Animals: how animals survive in hot deserts
core.p: Desert animals face heat, lack of water and little food. Their adaptations can be grouped into **structural** (body features), **behavioural** (what they do) and **physiological** (how the body works). Many are **nocturnal** and spend the day in burrows or shade, avoiding the hottest part of the day. Some get most of their water from **food** rather than drinking, and many produce **concentrated urine and dry droppings** to reduce water loss. Colour and body shape help them stay cool or hidden.

bullets: **Food chain** example: cactus or seeds, kangaroo rat, snake or fox, bird of prey.
**Producers** are sparse, so each animal needs a large home range.
**Decomposers** are few because of dry conditions, so little nutrient recycling occurs.
**Fragile ecosystem**: low productivity and slow recovery after damage.
Human activities such as **overgrazing, over-cultivation and vehicle use** damage the thin soils and plant cover.
**Rare rain** triggers rapid blooms of ephemeral plants, supporting insects and animals briefly.
This fragility links to **desertification** (a later spec point).

Figure 5 (bottom) shows the chain of linked parts: climate controls water, water and climate control soil, soil controls plants, plants feed animals, and people use all of them, so over-use by people can feed back into desertification.
core.h: Interdependence and the fragile desert ecosystem
core.p: Even with few resources, hot deserts form **ecosystems** where plants, animals and the physical environment depend on each other. Plants are the **producers**, supporting herbivores such as rodents and insects, which are eaten by predators such as foxes and snakes. With little water, the system is **fragile**: small changes such as **overgrazing**, vehicle damage or **climate change** can upset the balance. Recovery is slow because plants grow slowly and soils are thin.

bullets: **Farming**: **irrigation** schemes, such as the **Indira Gandhi Canal** in the Thar, bring water from Himalayan rivers so crops can be grown; crops such as wheat and cotton in irrigated areas.
**Mineral extraction**: Rajasthan has deposits such as **gypsum, limestone and building stone**; mining creates jobs.
**Energy**: **solar farms** use plentiful sunshine, for example large solar parks in Rajasthan, and **wind farms** can be used too.
**Tourism**: attractions such as camel safaris, desert festivals and historic towns like Jaisalmer bring visitors and jobs.
**Economic benefits**: income, jobs and improved services.
These opportunities rely on **water, technology and investment**.
In an exam, always **develop** each opportunity: say what it is and why the desert is suited to it.
core.p: Despite harsh conditions, hot deserts offer **opportunities for development**. Using a case study such as the **Thar Desert in Rajasthan, India**, you can explain how people use the desert for **farming, mineral extraction, energy and tourism**. The strong, reliable sunshine and open land are ideal for **solar power**, while irrigation allows crops where water can be supplied. Minerals and fossil fuels beneath the surface are valuable exports. Tourism can bring in money by using the unique landscape and culture.

bullets: **Extreme temperatures**: heat stress for workers, high energy demand for air conditioning, and damage to equipment; cold nights.
**Water supply**: little rainfall, **groundwater depletion**, competition between farming, industry and people.
**Inaccessibility**: long distances, few roads, high transport costs, sand blocking routes.
**Poor soils** and **salinisation** reduce farming yields.
**Sparse population** means small markets and a lack of workers and services.
**Environmental risks**: overuse of water and land can lead to **desertification**.
**Cost**: building infrastructure and getting water is expensive, so investment is needed.
Challenges and opportunities should be linked: 'solar power is possible but long transmission lines to cities are costly'.
Figure 5 (table) pairs each opportunity in the Thar Desert with a matching challenge, which is the structure the examiner wants in an extended answer.
core.p: Developing hot deserts is difficult because of the **extreme climate, water shortage and isolation**. Extreme heat makes working outdoors dangerous and increases the cost of cooling buildings and machines. **Water supply** is the biggest problem: surface water is rare, groundwater can be deep or run out, and irrigation can cause **salinisation**. Remote locations mean **inaccessibility**, so roads, railways and power lines are expensive to build and maintain, and sand can block them. Poor soils, rare floods, and limited services hold back development.

bullets: Give **where** it is (country, region and nearby features) and a **climate fact** with figures.
Name **one or two projects** (such as the Indira Gandhi Canal or a named solar park).
Explain **why** each opportunity is suited to the desert (for example flat land and strong Sun for solar).
Explain **why** each challenge occurs (for example distance from markets causes high transport costs).
Include **both positive and negative** consequences for local people and the environment.
If unsure of a detail, keep it general rather than inventing a figure.
Practise a **6 mark** answer with an introduction, development of two or three points, and a conclusion.
core.h: Case study guidance: how to write about a hot desert
core.p: The AQA specification asks for a **named case study** of a hot desert environment, so use place-specific detail rather than general statements. You should be able to give the **location**, **physical characteristics** (climate, soils, vegetation), **opportunities** (such as farming, minerals, energy, tourism) and **challenges** (such as heat, water supply and inaccessibility). If you studied a different desert in class (for example the Sahara), use the examples your teacher gave you, because the exam rewards accurate specific facts. Place names, figures and named projects lift answers into the top levels.

bullets: **Describe**: highest temperature (month and value), lowest temperature, range, total rainfall and seasonal pattern.
**Calculate** range = highest minus lowest; annual total = add the 12 monthly bars.
**Explain** with 'because' linking to sinking air, clear skies, or continentality.
Include **units**: degrees Celsius and millimetres.
Link **adaptations** to **conditions**: 'Cactus have spines because small surface area reduces water loss'.
**Compare** with the rainforest: deserts are hot and dry, with sparse vegetation, while rainforests are hot and wet with dense vegetation.
Use words such as **arid, sparse, nocturnal, xerophyte, diurnal range** correctly.
core.h: Exam skills: describing climate graphs and linking ideas
core.p: Climate graphs for hot deserts show **monthly temperature as a line** and **rainfall as bars**. To describe them well, give the **overall pattern**, quote **data with units**, and identify **anomalies**. For explanation, always link the **cause** (for example clear skies) to the **effect** (large temperature range). Top-level answers also link **climate to soils to vegetation to animals**: low rainfall leads to poor soils, which supports only sparse vegetation, which limits food for animals.

exam: **Describe the location**: say 'a belt 15 to 35 degrees north and south of the Equator, near the Tropics', and name at least one desert.
**2 mark 'Describe' climate**: give two linked facts with figures, for example low rainfall under 250 mm and a large daily temperature range.
**3 mark 'Explain' adaptation**: feature + how it works + why it helps (for example spines, small surface area, less water lost).
**4 mark 'Explain how'**: two developed adaptations, each with a link word such as 'so' or 'which means'.
**Graph skills**: read maximum and minimum temperature, calculate range, and add monthly rainfall for the total; always quote units.
**6 mark 'Assess'** opportunities and challenges: include at least two of each, linked to the case study with place detail, and finish with a judgement.
Use **specific vocabulary**: xerophyte, nocturnal, transpiration, arid, diurnal range.
Link **climate to vegetation to animals** to show understanding of the ecosystem as a whole.
Avoid **'it is hot and dry'** only; add numbers and reasons.
**Compare** with other biomes such as rainforest or cold environments if asked, highlighting differences in rainfall, temperature and vegetation.
Make a clear **judgement** in extended answers, supported by a reason and a counterpoint ('however').

mistakes.r: The hump stores fat, which is a food energy store; camels survive by tolerating water loss and drinking large amounts.
Many deserts are rocky or stony, and nights can be very cold, giving a large diurnal temperature range.
mistakes.w: Deserts are always sandy and hot all the time.

mistakes.r: Hot deserts have very low and unreliable rainfall, usually below 250 mm a year, often falling in short heavy storms.
mistakes.w: Deserts have no rain at all.

mistakes.r: Spines also reduce surface area and so reduce water loss by transpiration; they protect the plant as well.
mistakes.w: Cacti have spines to keep animals away only.

mistakes.r: Hot deserts are around 30 degrees north and south, where air descends, warms and dries, creating high pressure and clear skies.
mistakes.w: Deserts are hot because they are near the Equator.

mistakes.r: Large ears have many blood vessels near the surface and lose body heat, helping the fox stay cool; they also help hearing.
mistakes.w: Large ears on a fennec fox are for hearing only.

mistakes.r: Water supply, extreme heat, inaccessibility and poor soils make development costly and difficult.
mistakes.w: Development is easy because deserts are empty land.

mistakes.r: Quote key values with units, identify the pattern, give the range and then link to the cause.
mistakes.w: Describing a graph by just copying the numbers.

summary: The specification asks you to know where hot deserts are found and why, their climate, soils, vegetation and animals, how living things are adapted to heat and lack of water, and the opportunities and challenges of development in a named hot desert. It matters because exam questions test both description and explanation of adaptations and development.

terms.d: An arid environment with very low rainfall (under about 250 mm a year) and high temperatures.
A very dry condition caused by low rainfall and high evaporation.
A plant adapted to survive in very dry conditions.
Loss of water vapour from plant leaves through pores called stomata.
The difference between the highest daytime temperature and the lowest night-time temperature.
Active at night and resting during the day.
Incoming solar radiation reaching the Earth's surface.
A long, deep main root that reaches water far below the surface.
The build-up of salts in the soil, often caused by evaporation of irrigation water.
A sudden, short-lived flood following heavy rain, common on hard dry desert surfaces.
A feature or behaviour that helps an organism survive in its environment.
Artificially supplying water to land to grow crops.
Zone of descending air around 30 degrees latitude that causes dry conditions.
The variety of plant and animal species in an area.
Difficulty of reaching a place because of distance or poor transport.
The process by which land becomes more desert-like, usually caused by human activity and climate change.
The large-scale circulation in which air rises at the Equator, flows away at height, sinks at about 30 degrees latitude and returns near the surface; the sinking air causes dry conditions.
The upper level of underground water; deep tap roots and wells reach it in desert areas.

worked.ans: Cacti have spines instead of broad leaves. This gives a small surface area, so less water is lost by transpiration, helping the plant conserve water in the dry climate. Some plants, such as mesquite, have very long tap roots. These reach deep water tables underground, so the plant can get water even when there is no rain at the surface. (4 marks)

worked.q: A hot desert has a highest monthly mean temperature of 42 degrees Celsius in July and a lowest of 14 degrees in January. Calculate the annual temperature range. (1 mark)

worked.ans: During the day the skies are clear, so there is strong insolation and the surface heats rapidly to over 40 degrees Celsius. At night the same clear, dry air has little cloud or humidity to trap heat, so heat is quickly lost to space and temperatures fall close to 0 degrees. This produces a very big difference between day and night temperatures. (3 marks)
